hook_text: In 1910, in many villages, almost every young man was hundreds of kilometres away underground.
clip_script: The gold mines needed workers, hundreds of thousands of them. But not their families. Men from the Eastern Cape, Lesotho and Mozambique signed contracts, travelled to Johannesburg and lived in compounds with other men for months. At home, women did everything: ploughing, herding, building, raising children. Grandmothers raised grandchildren. Fathers were strangers. Money came home and paid for taxes, food and school fees. But sickness came home too: tuberculosis from crowded compounds and dusty tunnels. Why this system? Because the mines could pay a wage for one man, while the village fed his family. The families paid part of the cost of gold. And for generations, South African families were shaped by distance.
visual_style: A whiteboard drawing of a family split by a long road, with a compound and mine headgear on one side and a village with women ploughing on the other, coins and a cough cloud travelling along the road.
pacing: Gentle, with pauses on the village scenes.
